title: Optimize Guardrails - internal design review (gating, timeouts, overrides, baselines)
summary: Cross-functional review of the proposed quality guardrails gating for Optimize-driven config changes. Team aligned on enforcing gating in the control plane with staged rollout (observe-only → soft-block w/ override → hard-block), but open questions remained on (1) how long the apply flow should wait vs return pending/timeout, (2) override pathway and approvals + audit requirements, and (3) baseline strategy (backfill vs on-demand) and statistical guardrails for low-sample suites. SRE raised concerns about eval-runner backlog and safe-degrade behavior. Applied ML emphasized minimum sample size and CI-based thresholds to reduce flakiness, plus targeted sentinel prompts for formatting/tool-calling regressions. Telemetry discussed cardinality constraints for metric labels and the minimum fields needed for audit events.
topics: Enforcement point: control plane vs console vs runtime
Gating decision states: pass / fail / pending / timeout / error
Timeout semantics and safe-degrade behavior when eval runner is unhealthy
Override policy: RBAC, justification, optional second approver, rate limits
Baseline strategy: backfill top routes, prompt set revisions, threshold versioning
Stats methodology: min sample sizes, confidence intervals, flaky graders/rubrics
Telemetry + audit logs: event fields, PII redaction, cardinality and retention
Rollout: observe-only logging, canary, design partners, then default-on
action_items: Ethan Park - Propose final apply-time timeout behavior (UI/API) including pending/async path; include tier-specific safe-degrade recommendation - Due 2025-01-20
Jordan Lee - Draft policy evaluation pseudo-code for min sample size + CI rule + deterministic ordering; share in ADR comments - Due 2025-01-21
Selene Huang - Provide a short list of sentinel prompts for (a) tool-calling JSON formatting drift and (b) structured output schema compliance - Due 2025-01-22
Sana Farid - Recommend initial default thresholds for pilot (2–3 suites) and guidance for low-sample workloads; include rerun criteria for flaky results - Due 2025-01-22
Sean Gallagher - Define SRE alerting/paging proposal for eval runner backlog and timeout rates; include rollback trigger thresholds - Due 2025-01-23
Logan Wright - Confirm audit event + metrics label set that avoids high-cardinality (no prompt IDs) and is PII-safe; share a one-pager - Due 2025-01-23
Aditya Rao - Decide (with Security) whether overrides require a second approver for enterprise tiers, and what copy shows in Console for blocked applies - Due 2025-01-24
next_steps: Follow-up 30-min decision meeting focused only on timeout + pending behavior and safe-degrade by tier
Applied ML to circulate pilot suites + minimum prompt set coverage targets by product surface (chat/tool/structured)
Platform to update the enforcement ADR with override requirements and audit fields
SRE to add a lightweight load test plan for eval runner concurrency limits before pilot
transcript:
Meeting: Optimize Guardrails - internal design review (gating, timeouts, overrides, baselines)
Recorded: 2025-01-16 18:05 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Aditya Rao, Jonas Weber, Selene Huang, Sana Farid, Ethan Park, Jordan Lee, Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman

Auto-summary (Fireflies):
- Team reviewed the gating flow for Optimize config applies.
- Open questions: timeout behavior, override approvals, baseline/backfill plan.


[00:00] Aditya Rao: Alright, thanks everyone. Goal today is to walk through the design as it stands and get decisions—or at least narrow—on three hairy bits: timeouts, overrides, and baseline strategy. We’ve got a pilot window we told, uh, a couple design partners.

[00:18] Ethan Park: Cool. I can share screen mentally. The high level: Optimize generates a proposal, user hits Apply, control plane receives the apply request, policy engine evaluates whether gating is required, then we kick an eval run via the runner service. We store the gating result and either allow the config mutation or block.

[00:38] Jordan Lee: Emphasis: enforcement in control plane, not in console. Console just calls Apply and renders results.

[00:45] Sean Gallagher: And when the runner is on fire, the control plane becomes the blast radius, so we need crisp failure modes.

[00:52] Aditya Rao: Yeah. So, first: enforcement point. Any last objections to control plane?

[01:00] Jonas Weber: Applied ML is fine with control plane. It’s the most auditable place. Runtime enforcement is… hard to reason about if you want a single decision record tied to a prompt set revision.

[01:13] Selene Huang: +1. Also console-only is basically unenforceable if folks are using API.

[01:19] Aditya Rao: Great. Assume control plane. Next: what does Apply do while evals run? Today we spec’d “synchronous up to X seconds, then timeout state.” But I’m not sure that’s right.

[01:34] Ethan Park: Right now, our draft is: Apply request blocks for up to 90 seconds waiting for the eval runner. If the job hasn’t completed, we return “timeout/pending” and do not apply. User can come back and click “recheck” or “apply after complete.”

[01:51] Rafael Mendes: 90 seconds is long and also short. It’s long for user experience, short for evals if the queue is backed up.

[02:00] Sean Gallagher: The queue will be backed up sometimes. If we do synchronous waiting, we amplify the problem—more concurrent waiting requests, more load. The safe thing is an async state: return a run_id quickly.

[02:13] Aditya Rao: But product-wise we really want “one click apply,” not “start a job then poll.”

[02:20] Logan Wright: Polling is fine if we keep it behind the scenes. Console can open a modal that updates, but the API will see it.

[02:29] Jordan Lee: We can do a hybrid: Apply creates an eval run and returns 202 Accepted with run_id if it’s not finished in, say, 5–10 seconds. If it finishes quickly, we return pass/fail inline.

[02:44] Sana Farid: Statistically, we also might rerun a flaky suite. That means some runs will take longer by design.

[02:51] Jonas Weber: Yeah, and for quantization guardrails, suites are heavier. If we’re measuring rubric scores, it can be minutes.

[02:58] Aditya Rao: OK. So maybe the “apply” endpoint becomes “request apply” and then “finalize apply” once gating passes?

[03:07] Ethan Park: That’s a bigger API change. Another route: Apply endpoint does: if gating required and no cached result, return “blocked_pending_eval” plus run_id. Then we add a “re-attempt apply” endpoint that checks the stored result.

[03:22] Sean Gallagher: From SRE: make it impossible that we apply without a stored decision. No best-effort.

[03:29] Selene Huang: Agree. We need the decision artifact: suite list, prompt set revision, model version, config diff.

[03:38] Aditya Rao: Let’s park the API naming. The key question: if we don’t have a gating result yet, do we ever allow apply? Like for enterprise tiers during runner outage?

[03:49] Sean Gallagher: My vote: default is block. Runner down means no applies. Otherwise you’re basically turning off the whole point under stress.

[03:57] Rafael Mendes: There might be an exec exception for, like, Dedicated customer incident. But it should be a manual approval path, not “automatic bypass.”

[04:08] Jordan Lee: That maps to policy: safe-degrade behavior is itself a policy decision by tier. We can encode “when runner unavailable: require override” vs “hard block.”

[04:20] Aditya Rao: OK but what’s “unavailable”? Like error rate > X? backlog > Y? timeouts?

[04:27] Sean Gallagher: We can define “gating health” SLO: worker queue depth, p95 job latency, error rate. But please don’t put a ton of moving parts in the apply path.

[04:38] Ethan Park: Implementation-wise: apply calls runner. If runner returns 5xx or times out, we mark the gating run as “system_error” and apply blocks unless override permitted.

[04:52] Logan Wright: For metrics, we should differentiate “eval_failed_quality” from “eval_failed_system.” Otherwise dashboards are confusing.

[05:01] Nadia Rahman: And for cost reporting, we need to know how many applies were blocked due to system vs quality. It changes interpretation.

[05:09] Aditya Rao: Great point. So we need separate states.

[05:14] Selene Huang: Also please, don’t call it “quality failed” in UI if it’s a system timeout.

[05:19] Aditya Rao: Yep.

[05:22] Aditya Rao: Second big topic: overrides. The working idea: soft-block stage allows override with justification, restricted roles. Hard-block stage: no override, or override but requiring approval?

[05:36] Jordan Lee: If we allow override during hard-block, it’s not really hard-block. But we can implement two-person integrity: request override, approver in another role approves, audit log writes both.

[05:49] Sean Gallagher: That’s operationally heavy. In oncall, you want a button that works. But I get the compliance angle.

[05:56] Ethan Park: Technically, we can require an approver for certain tenants (enterprise). For internal canary maybe single approver is fine.

[06:05] Jonas Weber: Applied ML concern: if overrides become common, you can ship regressions. We should track override rate and investigate.

[06:14] Sana Farid: Also: override should be tied to a reason category. Like “false positive suspected” vs “urgent business need.” Otherwise the data is useless.

[06:24] Logan Wright: Please keep reason categories low-cardinality. Like 5 values, not freeform tags.

[06:30] Aditya Rao: We can do both: dropdown reason + freeform justification box.

[06:36] Rafael Mendes: And rate limit overrides. If someone overrides 50 times, something’s wrong.

[06:43] Sean Gallagher: Rate limit per tenant per day maybe. Plus an alert.

[06:49] Aditya Rao: OK. Let’s move to baseline strategy. Today the proposal is: for any apply, run evals comparing “current config” vs “proposed config.” But we don’t always have a baseline for “current,” especially if prompt sets changed.

[07:06] Selene Huang: Right. We should treat “baseline” as: the currently serving config on that route, on that model version, with prompt set revision N, and suite S. If we don’t have it, we either compute on demand or accept a less strict check.

[07:23] Jonas Weber: From Evals perspective: it’s best if we have a stored baseline for top routes, so apply-time is only computing the delta config.

[07:32] Sana Farid: But you still need paired evaluation if you want a strong claim. Comparing to an old baseline is tricky if the grader changed.

[07:41] Jordan Lee: Policy engine can require “baseline freshness”: baseline must be within X days and same prompt set revision.

[07:49] Ethan Park: That increases eval load significantly if prompt sets rev often.

[07:54] Selene Huang: Prompt sets shouldn’t rev daily. But they will rev sometimes. We need an explicit lifecycle.

[08:01] Logan Wright: I’m worried about storing per-prompt outputs. That’s huge and also PII-ish.

[08:07] Jonas Weber: We don’t need to store raw prompts in telemetry. But eval artifacts may contain them.

[08:12] Aditya Rao: We’ve said: prompt sets are customer-provided sometimes. We need retention and redaction policies.

[08:18] Sean Gallagher: For internal pilot: can we just keep artifacts in an internal bucket and purge after 14 days?

[08:25] Ethan Park: We can. But audit logs should keep minimal fields longer.

[08:30] Logan Wright: Yes. Separate “artifact storage” (short) from “audit summary” (long). Audit summary contains metrics + versions, not prompts.

[08:41] Nadia Rahman: Also cost: we need to link the config change to cost deltas later. Not today, but soon.

[08:47] Aditya Rao: OK. Back to baselines. Proposed plan (draft): Phase 1 backfill baselines for top N Optimize recommendations—like the most-used routes. Everyone OK?

[08:58] Jonas Weber: That’s good. But define “top N” by what? token volume? apply attempts? revenue?

[09:06] Aditya Rao: Probably token volume + number of tenants. Nadia you probably have thoughts.

[09:12] Nadia Rahman: Token volume weighted by revenue tier. Also exclude routes with custom prompts we don’t have rights to run, unless customer opt-in.

[09:24] Selene Huang: For customer prompt sets, we can do “bring your own prompt set” and baseline only exists if they uploaded.

[09:32] Jordan Lee: Then policy should say: if no prompt set coverage for that workload, gating required but will fail with “insufficient coverage.” Or block? That’s a product decision.

[09:43] Aditya Rao: This is a key UX point: if we block applies because they didn’t upload prompt sets, they’ll hate it.

[09:50] Sean Gallagher: But if we don’t have any coverage, we’re flying blind.

[09:54] Jonas Weber: We can offer default Redwood prompt sets by workload type. Not perfect but better than nothing.

[10:03] Selene Huang: Yep. For structured output and tool calling, we can provide sentinel sets. It catches formatting regressions which are common with quantization.

[10:12] Sana Farid: We need to be explicit: sentinel sets mainly cover “format adherence” not “task success.” So thresholds must reflect that.

[10:21] Aditya Rao: Great. Let’s talk thresholds / stats briefly. Sana can you outline the approach?

[10:27] Sana Farid: Sure. Proposed default: For each metric, we define a regression threshold in delta terms relative to baseline, plus minimum sample size. For continuous rubric scores: require the lower bound of 95% CI on delta to be above -X. For binary success rates: same idea, Wilson interval. If sample size < min_n, gating result is “inconclusive” and blocks unless override.

[10:53] Jordan Lee: That “inconclusive blocks” is important: determinism. Otherwise we’ll have edge cases where it passes sometimes.

[11:00] Sean Gallagher: But “inconclusive blocks” might spike if suites are small. That’s a lot of blocked applies.

[11:07] Sana Farid: That’s why we pick min_n carefully per suite. For pilot, keep suites small but stable; for GA, we should increase coverage.

[11:18] Jonas Weber: Also graders can be flaky. If we use LLM-as-judge, model updates can change distributions.

[11:26] Selene Huang: For pilot, we should pin judge model versions.

[11:30] Ethan Park: Pinning means we need to store judge version in gating result schema.

[11:36] Logan Wright: Also in audit events.

[11:39] Aditya Rao: OK.

[11:42] Aditya Rao: Back to timeouts. Let’s try to converge. Sean, what’s acceptable from SRE?

[11:49] Sean Gallagher: A) Apply endpoint should not hold open for minutes. B) We need clear queue limits and backpressure. C) If runner is degraded, apply should fail fast with “system unavailable” rather than hanging.

[12:04] Rafael Mendes: And Console should render a “pending” state if it’s just queued. But if it’s truly broken, show “try again later” and don’t encourage spam-click.

[12:16] Ethan Park: So: we do 10s sync wait. If job not done, return pending with run_id. Then Console polls every, say, 5s for up to 2 minutes, then tells user “still running” and offers to come back.

[12:33] Aditya Rao: That seems reasonable.

[12:36] Jordan Lee: One nuance: policy evaluation needs to be consistent across retries. If user re-attempts apply, they shouldn’t get a different suite list because tags changed.

[12:47] Selene Huang: That means suite selection inputs must be captured in the run record: workload tags, optimization type, model family.

[12:55] Ethan Park: Yep.

[12:57] Logan Wright: Please don’t include raw prompt lengths as labels. Use buckets.

[13:03] Aditya Rao: Good. Next nuance: caching eval results. If the exact same config delta was evaluated yesterday, can we reuse?

[13:12] Jonas Weber: Prefer yes, with invalidation when prompt set revision or model version changes.

[13:18] Sana Farid: Also invalidate if threshold version changes.

[13:22] Jordan Lee: That’s a lot of keys. But doable: cache key = (model version, prompt set rev, suite id, config delta hash, judge version). Threshold version doesn’t affect the raw metrics; it affects decision. So we can recompute decision from stored summary.

[13:39] Ethan Park: Exactly. Store metric aggregates + sample size. Policy engine re-evaluates.

[13:47] Aditya Rao: Great.

[13:49] Aditya Rao: Let’s do a quick walkthrough of states and copy. Selene, you had concerns about calling it timeout.

[13:56] Selene Huang: Yeah. “Timeout” sounds like we waited and gave up. Sometimes it’s just “still running.” Better states: “Pending evaluation” vs “Evaluation system error.” Then an explicit “Not enough samples” state.

[14:10] Aditya Rao: OK. For user: Pass = green, Fail = red with metric deltas. Pending = spinner with ETA-ish. System error = gray with retry.

[14:22] Sean Gallagher: Don’t promise ETA. That’s how you get yelled at.

[14:25] Aditya Rao: Fair.

[14:27] Jordan Lee: For API: return a machine-readable enum. Console can interpret.

[14:33] Logan Wright: And audit logs should store the enum too.

[14:36] Aditya Rao: Ok.

[14:38] Aditya Rao: Now, override path. Let’s decide: do we require second approver for enterprise in pilot?

[14:46] Sean Gallagher: In pilot, please no. It’s going to slow learning.

[14:50] Rafael Mendes: Agree. But ensure we can add it later without schema break.

[14:55] Jordan Lee: We can define override object fields now: requested_by, justification, reason_code, approved_by optional. If approved_by absent, it was self-approved in pilot.

[15:08] Ethan Park: But careful: we can’t put nested JSON in audit event payload if it’s too big—well, we can, but there are size limits.

[15:17] Logan Wright: Keep audit event fields flat: override_requested_by, override_approved_by, override_reason_code, override_justification_truncated.

[15:29] Aditya Rao: Makes sense.

[15:32] Jonas Weber: Another thing: When someone overrides, we should automatically schedule a post-change monitoring job. Like, run lightweight evals hourly for 24h.

[15:44] Sean Gallagher: That’s good but adds load. Maybe only for high-risk optimizations like quant.

[15:51] Selene Huang: Quant definitely.

[15:54] Aditya Rao: Ok. We’ll mark optimization types as risk levels.

[16:00] Nadia Rahman: And capture the optimization type in gating record; it’s needed for later ROI analysis.

[16:08] Aditya Rao: Good.

[16:10] Aditya Rao: Alright, jump to quantization specifically. Selene, can you summarize known failure modes?

[16:18] Selene Huang: Mostly: formatting drift (JSON not parseable, missing keys), tool call arguments become sloppy, and reasoning degradation where it starts hallucinating step count or losing long-context references. The formatting drift shows up quickly with sentinel prompts.

[16:36] Jonas Weber: There’s also “refusal rate changes” sometimes—model gets more conservative when quantized.

[16:42] Sana Farid: That’s measurable with a refusal classifier, but we need stable definitions.

[16:48] Jordan Lee: For policy: quant transitions require a mandatory suite list. That list is fixed by model family.

[16:56] Ethan Park: We’ll encode “quantization transition rules” separate from generic thresholds, I think.

[17:02] Aditya Rao: OK.

[17:04] Aditya Rao: SRE concerns: runner backlog, isolation from customer traffic.

[17:10] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. Don’t run eval traffic in the same cluster pool as customer inference, or at least separate queues with quotas. Otherwise gating will steal GPUs.

[17:21] Ethan Park: Our current runner uses a dedicated worker pool and submits inference requests tagged “eval.” Runtime can route to a reserved capacity. That’s the plan.

[17:31] Rafael Mendes: Then the critical metric is “eval job queue depth.” We need alerts before it becomes user-visible.

[17:39] Logan Wright: We can emit: guardrails_eval_jobs_queued, guardrails_eval_job_latency_ms p50/p95, guardrails_apply_pending_count.

[17:50] Jordan Lee: Also “decision determinism” metric? Like, same input yields same output. But that’s more of a test.

[17:57] Aditya Rao: Let’s not add too many new metrics; just the ones we need for paging.

[18:02] Sean Gallagher: Paging: error rate, queue depth above threshold, and sustained p95 above, say, 10 minutes.

[18:12] Aditya Rao: OK.

[18:14] (crosstalk)

[18:15] Nadia Rahman: One more: we should correlate post-apply customer quality signals. Like support tickets, thumbs down.

[18:22] Aditya Rao: Yep, but that’s later.

[18:25] Jonas Weber: For baseline strategy, I want to revisit: paired evaluation. If we’re doing cached baseline + new config, we should make sure we compare on identical prompt subset.

[18:36] Sana Farid: Exactly. If prompt set changes, you can’t compare deltas meaningfully.

[18:41] Ethan Park: That implies our “baseline record” is basically an eval run summary. If prompt set rev changes, you need a new baseline.

[18:50] Selene Huang: Which is OK if prompt sets rev infrequently. But we need a policy: prompt set revisions are explicit and controlled.

[18:59] Aditya Rao: So a prompt set is like a versioned artifact. Customers can upload a new version, but it becomes effective only when pinned.

[19:08] Jordan Lee: Yes. Pinning is important for determinism and audit.

[19:12] Logan Wright: Please, pinning doesn’t mean we store prompts in event logs.

[19:16] Aditya Rao: Understood.

[19:18] Aditya Rao: Let’s capture decisions so far:
- Control plane enforcement.
- Hybrid sync/async apply: wait ~10s then return pending with run_id.
- States: pass/fail/pending/system_error/insufficient_samples.
- Overrides allowed in soft-block stage; pilot no second approver, but schema supports later.
- System error blocks unless override allowed by policy.
- Baselines backfilled for top routes; baseline tied to prompt set revision.

Anything missing?

[19:55] Sean Gallagher: We need to decide default safe-degrade per tier. Like, Hosted self-serve: block. Dedicated enterprise: allow override. Something like that.

[20:06] Aditya Rao: That’s a product + leadership decision. I’ll take it.

[20:10] Jordan Lee: Also: we should define “minimum sample sizes” per suite. If we set min_n too high, everyone hits insufficient.

[20:18] Sana Farid: I’ll propose initial values for pilot.

[20:21] Selene Huang: I’ll also give the sentinel prompt list.

[20:24] Ethan Park: And I’ll update the apply endpoint spec.

[20:28] Logan Wright: I’ll do the cardinality review in parallel.

[20:31] Aditya Rao: Great.

[20:34] (small pause)

[20:36] Aditya Rao: One more point: audit logs. We’ve had customer asks about proving eval ran before changes. We should capture: who initiated, config diff, gating run id, suite ids, threshold version, decision reasons, and override.

[20:55] Jordan Lee: For “decision reasons,” we should store structured failure reasons. Like “metric X lower bound below threshold,” “min_n not met,” etc.

[21:05] Ethan Park: We’ll store an array. But arrays in audit events—size.

[21:10] Logan Wright: We can store top 5 reasons, truncated. Full details in gating run artifact store.

[21:17] Jonas Weber: Full details should include per-metric stats and confidence intervals.

[21:23] Aditya Rao: OK.

[21:25] Sean Gallagher: Also: audit log export to SIEM—some enterprises ask. Keep that in mind.

[21:31] Aditya Rao: Yup.

[21:33] Aditya Rao: Any last concerns?

[21:37] Rafael Mendes: Just: avoid using the word “regression” in UI for system errors. Support will get tickets.

[21:44] Selene Huang: And please add a “rerun evaluation” action. Some fails will be noise.

[21:51] Sana Farid: Rerun should be limited. Otherwise they’ll rerun until it passes.

[21:56] Jordan Lee: Policy can limit reruns per day or require override after N reruns.

[22:02] Aditya Rao: Good call.

[22:05] Aditya Rao: Ok we’re at time. I’ll send notes and schedule a quick follow-up just on timeouts/safe-degrade. Thanks all.

[22:15] (meeting ends abruptly; some audio continues)

[22:17] Speaker 2: Wait did we decide ten seconds or fifteen?

[22:20] Aditya Rao: Ten for now. We can adjust.

[22:22] Sean Gallagher: Yeah please ten.

[22:25] End.
